red_rule.rationale: Maryland sets no fixed public advisory period: a public advisory stays in effect until the local health department finds that sampling of the receiving water has returned to normal or prior background levels (COMAR 26.08.10.08D). Operators must report an overflow or plant bypass to MDE and the local health department within 24 hours and notify the public within 24 hours when it reaches shellfish, drinking-water, bathing-beach or recreation waters (Env. § 9-331.1; COMAR 26.08.10.03 and .08A). Local practice: Anne Arundel County closes affected waters for about a week after a sewage spill; MDE advises avoiding swimming within 48 hours of heavy rain
red_rule.source: Md. Code, Environment § 9-331.1; COMAR 26.08.10.03, .08A and .08D; Anne Arundel County Department of Health closings and advisories; MDE Healthy Beaches

yellow_rule.rationale: We use 96 hours after the reported discharge end for lakes. The cited research shows that bacteria can persist in still water and sediment. This is a site caution period, not a measured recovery time.
yellow_rule.source: Environment Agency (England), report SC250004/R (2026); Korajkic et al. (2019)

red_rule.rationale: Virginia law places no public notice duty on the discharger: an overflow must be reported to DEQ or the local emergency services office within 24 hours (Va. Code § 62.1-44.5 B; 9VAC25-31-190 L 6 and 7), and DEQ passes the report to the Department of Health, the media and its email and social lists only when VDH or DEQ finds a risk to health or water use, with no deadline (§ 62.1-44.19:6 B). Where an operator publishes its own post-overflow period it is applied under that operator's name

yellow_rule.rationale: Combined sewer discharges contain sewage and rainwater. EPA documents high bacteria levels in these discharges. We use a caution period of 72 hours after the reported end; the reported volume does not establish bacteria levels at a particular spot.
yellow_rule.source: U.S. EPA, Report to Congress on Impacts and Control of Combined Sewer Overflows and Sanitary Sewer Overflows (2004)
